description: Our goal is to build something useful with real NASA data, learn as much as we can along the way and show our work at the national and international level. We care about getting the science right and explaining it clearly. We are looking for people who can write English, edit video, or know earth science or space weather.
summary: Earth's air weighs 1,033 grams over every square centimetre of ground. The air on Mars weighs about 19. DERIN asks how much rock can stand in for that missing sky at Apollinaris Sulci, a human landing site that Kerber and colleagues proposed in 2015, with homes dug into wind-carved yardangs as people did in Cappadocia. DERIN is a browser simulator built on a real NASA HiRISE terrain model. Click a slope, place a room, and read the radiation dose, rock load, air loss and heat, each with a range and a tag: measured, modelled or assumed. About 5.75 m of rock, measured from the slope, matches the mass of Earth's atmosphere and gives 0.82 mSv a year at the room wall, inside Earth's 0.70 to 0.87. Rock cannot hold cabin pressure or air, and it takes only part of the heat. Derinkuyu, an underground city in Türkiye, is the Earth analog: its measured temperatures show where the comparison holds and where it breaks.
details:
What DERIN does

DERIN answers one question for a crew on Mars: how much rock do we need, and what can that rock not do for us? It works on one real place, a yardang slope at Apollinaris Sulci (about 12.48° S, 177.97° E), 74 km east of the landing site proposed by Kerber et al. (2015). Kerber's team and Arai (2013) proposed rock-cut homes on Mars modelled on Cappadocia. The idea is theirs. DERIN adds the numbers for this site.

How it works

The simulator runs in any browser and sends nothing anywhere. It loads a NASA HiRISE digital terrain model at 2 m per post. The user clicks a slope to place a door and drags a room into the rock. For every point, DERIN casts rays in all directions and adds up the rock along each one, because cosmic rays arrive from the whole sky and the thinnest path to the sky sets the dose. Depth is measured from the slope, not straight down. The dose model uses the published depth-dose curves of Zhang et al. (2022) at the site's air pressure (691 Pa, Mars Climate Database). Heat, rock load, air leakage and the crew's whole-mission dose update on every change. Each number shows its range and its tag, and a click opens the formula and the source. Ten sheets: Site, Verdict, Room, Crew, Sky, Derinkuyu, Sensors, Bench, plus "From the room" and "Where to dig". "Play the argument" runs the whole case in 30 seconds on the live engine. English and Turkish.

What it found

- Mass: Earth's air column is 1,033 g/cm². Mars has about 19 here. 5.75 m of rock at 1.765 g/cm³ makes up the difference (5.4 to 8.5 m across published densities).

- Dose against depth (solar minimum, modelled): 247 mSv a year on the surface, 19 at 3 m, 5.7 at 4 m, 1.65 at 5 m. A factor-of-two error in the curve moves the depth by only about 0.6 m.

- At the default door (60° slope, 15.3 m of rock straight up, 5.75 m from the slope) the room wall gets 0.82 mSv a year (range 0.34 to 5.66). Earth's ground, all natural external sources: 0.70 to 0.87.

- Equal mass is not equal dose: at 1,033 g/cm² the published curves give Mars rock about 2 times the cosmic dose of Earth air.

- The slope matters: under the same 5 m of vertical rock, a 30° slope gives 1.94 times the flat-ground dose and a 60° slope 11.7 times. From the room, 5.1% of the sky brings half of the dose.

- The best door on this block reaches a whole room under Earth's ground dose after a 6.2 m tunnel. A straight open tunnel lets dose in, so it needs a bend.

What rock cannot replace

- Pressure: the rock over the room presses down with 38 kPa against a 70 kPa cabin, so the module must carry its own load (balance only at 10.7 m).

- Air: bare porous rock would lose 847% of the room's air a day against a design limit of 0.05%. A liner tear drops the cabin from 70 to 50 kPa in about 6 minutes.

- Heat: the rock takes 1.05 of the 12.6 kW a working crew makes. The room overheats in 2.7 days and needs about 58 m² of radiator.

- Cruise: the whole mission gives one crew member 692 mSv (558 to 816) against NASA's 600 mSv career limit. The 360-day cruise alone brings 662 mSv, which no rock on Mars can change.

The Earth analog: Derinkuyu

Derinkuyu reaches about 40 m into soft volcanic tuff, like the soft Medusae Fossae rock at the site. The two match in rock mechanics and digging. They split on air and radiation. Measurements by Aydan and Ulusay (2013) show the seventh floor going from -1.7 °C in February to 9.2 °C in August. Conduction through rock alone would erase that yearly swing, so the city exchanges air with the surface. DERIN drives a one-way cold-air model with NASA POWER hourly temperatures. It fits the seventh floor within 0.90 K, but a plain sine fits as well (0.72 K), so monthly data cannot prove how the air moves; shaft airflow would. Going 40 m down at Derinkuyu changes the external dose by only about 8% (radon excluded), because Earth's sky already did that job. On Mars the rock must do it. These breaks are part of the result: Derinkuyu is a process analog for digging and living in soft tuff, not a radiation test.

What to measure first

NASA's Moon to Mars Architecture Definition Document (Rev C, Appendix E) lists data gap DN-001 M: the physical and mechanical properties of Martian rock. DERIN moves each unknown across its published range and ranks them: permeability changes the air loss 2,278 times, rock strength changes the deepest safe room 440 times, heat conductivity changes the heat answer 15 times. The Sensors sheet proposes a cheap field test: two pressure sensors in sealed chambers at 1 m and 2 m read the rock's permeability back from the daily pressure wave recorded by InSight, within 1% in 5 sols at low sensor noise.

Benefits and goals

Mission planners and students get a single place to see how deep a Mars room must go, why the slope matters as much as the depth, and which rock measurement would settle the most. Every claim carries its source and its uncertainty, so the tool shows where the evidence ends.

Tools

JavaScript (ES modules, Web Worker), three.js for the 3D terrain, GSAP for motion, Python and NumPy for data preparation, Geant4 11.4 for our own slope and equal-mass checks, Node.js test runner (76 engine tests). Hosted on GitHub Pages. Code written with Claude (Anthropic); see the README.

Limits

Dose-depth curves beyond about 100 g/cm² are models, not measurements. Rock density, strength, conductivity and permeability at this site have never been measured. Pits and narrow ridges are not validated. Radon and solar storms behind the rock are not modelled. The results are a screening study, not an engineering design.

Project Report: https://bdsyi07.github.io/derin/DERIN_Report_EN.pdf
